name: Victor Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a transmission crew, the big steel towers that carry the high-voltage lines across country. We work out of a base near the North Ridge substation, but half the month we're on the road, staying in cheap hotels near whatever stretch needs work. A normal day is a safety briefing at six, then climbing a tower, replacing insulators or spacers, or helping the helicopter team string new conductor. I love the height and the views, and the feeling that a whole city's lights go through the wire you're fixing. What wears me out is being away from the kids for a week at a time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And at home? How do you fit the job and the family together?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Samira teaches maths at a secondary school, so she's the steady one at home. We've got Yusuf, who's eleven, and Amina, who's eight. Mortgage on a three-bedroom on the edge of town, maybe five months saved if we're careful. I use AI every day, honestly: to plan routes, check the weather windows for climbing, summarise the job specs, even to help Yusuf with his homework over video call from the hotel. I'm a union rep for our crew and I'm left-leaning, but I don't think the answer is to fight the technology. It's who owns it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, okay, it was a bubble, but the tools are still useful, so let's keep the good bits. I'd probably post something about how the useful stuff was always the boring stuff, scheduling and paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I'd be a little disappointed. I like these tools, and I'd hoped they'd take some of the travel and the inspection grind off us. But my job is safe, and I'd keep using the AI for what it's good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much changes. I'd keep using AI for planning and reports, and maybe show the older guys on the crew how to use it for their timesheets. Keep saving, keep the mortgage ticking down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down, the way you feel when a big match ends nil-nil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd show the older guys how to use it. Who's that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly Frank, who's been on towers for thirty years and hates screens. Last month I set up voice notes so he could do his job report by talking into his phone, and he loved it. That's the kind of small win I'd still want in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you have hoped AI would do that it doesn't do here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fly drones along the lines and spot the cracked insulators before we climb, so we only go up where we need to. That would mean fewer nights away. In this picture, we're still climbing every tower to look.

S0.say: It was a bubble, but the tools are still useful, so keep the good bits. The useful stuff was always the boring stuff, like scheduling and paperwork.
S0.think: He'd be a little disappointed, because he hoped AI would cut the travel and the inspection grind. His job is safe, and he'd keep using the tools for what they're good at.
S0.do: Keeps using AI daily for route planning, weather windows and reports. Helps older crew members like Frank use voice notes for job reports, and keeps saving and paying the mortgage.
S0.feel: Calm, slightly let down, like a big match that ends nil-nil.
S0.quote: Last month I set up voice notes so he could do his job report by talking into his phone, and he loved it.
S0.fieldNote: Victor is the rare lineworker who is disappointed when AI fizzles. He sees technology as a way to spend fewer nights away from his kids. His progressive views focus on ownership of technology rather than opposing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where unions matter most. The tech's coming, so let's bargain over it: retraining, no forced redundancies, and a share of the savings for the crews. I'd be bringing a proposal to the branch, not a protest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it could be good for me. If drones and AI do the inspection, the company needs people who can fly them, read the data and decide which tower to climb. I'd want to be that person. But I'd worry for the guys who can't make the jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a drone pilot licence in the first few months, and I'd pay for it myself if I had to, it's around nine hundred. I'd volunteer for every pilot project the company runs. And I'd write up a proposal for the union on how to share the work out fairly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited even. Though there's guilt in it, because I know Frank won't feel the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Nine hundred is a fair amount for your family. Would Samira agree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd ask me to show her the numbers, because she's a maths teacher. If I could show her it led to a better-paid role with fewer nights away, she'd agree. If I couldn't, she'd tell me to get the company to pay, and she'd be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd worry about the guys who can't make the jump. What would you do for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Push for the company to keep some climbing crews and give people like Frank a decent early pension deal if they want it. And pair people up, so younger ones learn the drone side and older ones teach the hands-on side. Nobody should be dumped.

S1.say: This is where unions matter most: the tech is coming, so bargain over retraining, no forced redundancies and a share of the savings. He'd bring the branch a proposal, not a protest.
S1.think: It could be good for him, because the company will need people who fly drones, read the data and decide which tower to climb. He worries for colleagues who can't make that jump.
S1.do: Gets a drone pilot licence within months, about nine hundred, and volunteers for every company pilot project. Writes a union proposal on sharing work fairly, including pairing young and old crew members.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, with some guilt about colleagues like Frank.
S1.quote: The tech's coming, so let's bargain over it: retraining, no forced redundancies, and a share of the savings for the crews.
S1.fieldNote: He moves first and sees opportunity, but frames it collectively rather than as a personal race. His wife acts as the check on his spending. His guilt about older colleagues was genuine and specific.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to slow the rollout and make sure the gains are shared, fast. Public ownership of the robots that run the grid, a basic income, retraining that's paid. I'd say it calmly, but I'd say it everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, two years scares me, even though I like this stuff. If the drones and robots can do the whole job, then the drone pilot job I was planning for goes too, maybe in a year after the climbers. Being early doesn't help much if the whole ladder disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still get the drone licence fast, because it might buy me a year or two. I'd save everything I could, cancel our summer trip to see Samira's family, and push the union to negotiate phased redundancy with proper payouts. I'd also start asking around about jobs in grid safety oversight, because someone has to answer for the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still feel like I had some moves, but fewer than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Yusuf and Amina?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yusuf's already asked me if AI will do everything. I'd tell him that the world is changing fast, that his dad's going to have to learn new things, and that's okay. Amina's eight, she'd just want to know if we're still getting a puppy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Cancelling the trip to Samira's family is a big one. Why that first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's the biggest chunk, about two thousand with flights. It'd hurt, her mum's not young. But I'd rather explain that than miss a mortgage payment. We'd do a long video call instead and promise them the next year.

S2.say: We need to slow the rollout and share the gains fast: public ownership of grid robots, a basic income and paid retraining. He'd say it calmly but everywhere.
S2.think: Two years scares him even though he likes the technology, because the drone pilot role he planned for would vanish soon after the climbers. Being early doesn't help if the whole ladder goes.
S2.do: Gets the drone licence quickly to buy a year or two and saves hard, cancelling a two-thousand family trip. Pushes the union for phased redundancy with proper payouts and looks for grid safety oversight roles.
S2.feel: Anxious, still feeling he has some moves, but fewer than he'd like.
S2.quote: Being early doesn't help much if the whole ladder disappears.
S2.fieldNote: Even this adaptive, tech-friendly worker loses his confidence when the timeline is two years. He still looks for a role, in oversight, but knows it's thin cover. Cancelling the family trip clearly cost him emotionally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to do it right, if we start now. I'd say the robots running the grid should be publicly owned, so the savings come back as lower bills or shorter hours. I'd be on a union working group about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I think I could land somewhere useful. Robot fleets for the grid will need people to check their work, certify them, investigate when something goes wrong. That's a mix of hands-on knowledge and tech, which is exactly me. I'd be 48.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Drone licence this year, then a two-year part-time diploma in grid automation or safety. I'd also try to get onto the team that tests robots in the company, even unpaid hours at first. And save an extra three hundred a month, which means fewer takeaways on the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than not. It feels like a race I could win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't checking robot work the kind of thing AGI could do too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably, in the end. But I think people will want a human to sign off on high-voltage work for a while after the robots can technically do it, because when a tower fails, the whole region goes dark. That's my bet. I could be wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yusuf would be sixteen and Amina thirteen, so I could be away less or more without it mattering so much. And Samira's job feels safer than mine for a bit, people still want a teacher in the room. That gives us one steady income while I change lanes.

S3.say: Five years is enough to do it right if we start now, with publicly owned grid robots so savings come back as lower bills or shorter hours. He'd join a union working group.
S3.think: He thinks he can land in a role checking, certifying and investigating robot fleets, which mixes hands-on knowledge with tech. He admits AGI could eventually do that too.
S3.do: Gets the drone licence this year, then does a two-year part-time diploma in grid automation or safety. Tries to join the company's robot testing team and saves an extra three hundred a month.
S3.feel: Uneasy but more hopeful than not, like a race he could win.
S3.quote: When a tower fails, the whole region goes dark. That's my bet. I could be wrong.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Victor's adaptability returns as a real advantage. He was honest that his bet on human sign-off could be wrong. His wife's teaching job is his family's anchor during the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to build a fairer system, and it'd be a scandal to waste it. I'd want the union, the government and the companies all at one table from year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels workable. I could ride the transition all the way: climber, drone pilot, robot supervisor, then maybe teaching or safety. I'd be 53, the kids grown. My worry is less me and more my town, and the guys who won't move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the drone licence and the diploma at a slower pace, one thing a year. I'd put a bit into a pension top-up and maybe some savings in index funds, which I've never done. And I'd help set up a union programme so every lineworker gets paid time to retrain, not just the keen ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can use. It feels like weather you can see coming over the hills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Index funds are new for you. Why now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if robots do most of the work, the people who own a slice of the companies do better than the people who don't. It feels a bit against my politics, honestly. But I'd rather my kids have a slice than nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a moment in that decade you picture clearly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the day I take Frank's grandson out to show him how we used to climb, while a robot's doing the actual tower. I'd want him to know people did this once, and did it well.

S4.say: Ten years is a real chance to build a fairer system, and wasting it would be a scandal. The union, the government and the companies should all be at one table from year one.
S4.think: Ten years feels workable, riding the change from climber to drone pilot to robot supervisor and then teaching or safety. His worry is more for his town and colleagues who won't move.
S4.do: Takes the drone licence and diploma at one step a year and starts a pension top-up and index fund savings for the first time. Helps set up a union programme for paid retraining time for every lineworker.
S4.feel: Uneasy in a usable way, like weather he can see coming over the hills.
S4.quote: It feels a bit against my politics, honestly. But I'd rather my kids have a slice than nothing.
S4.fieldNote: Victor sees a decade as enough to move step by step through several roles. He admitted investing in shares sits uneasily with his politics. His thoughts kept returning to colleagues and his town rather than himself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because even being early and keen doesn't help when there's no time. What would help is a basic income that kicks in fast, public ownership of the grid robots so the savings go back to people, and paid retraining time that counts as work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the travel. People think of the job, but for us the job is also nights away from family. If robots took the travel and left us the thinking, I'd sign up tomorrow.

headlineQuote: If robots took the travel and left us the thinking, I'd sign up tomorrow.
portrait: Victor Ibrahim is a 43-year-old transmission lineworker who climbs high-voltage towers and spends half the month on the road, with a maths-teacher wife, two kids and about five months saved. He uses AI daily and sees it as a way to spend fewer nights away, and as a union rep he wants to bargain over technology rather than fight it. Steady change looks like an opportunity to become a drone pilot, but fast AGI scares him because the whole ladder he planned to climb would disappear. With five or ten years he regains his footing and plans a step-by-step move into robot oversight, while worrying most for older colleagues and his town.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because being early and keen wouldn't help when there's no time to move into a new role.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income that starts fast, public ownership of grid robots so savings return to people, and paid retraining time that counts as work.
